question: Regulation (EU) No 1370/2007 identifies efficiency and safety as key pillars for ensuring a high-quality public transport service that is accessible to all1. However, a number of problems undermine this objective, including overcrowding and a growing concern for the safety of passengers and staff.

Frequent incidents of violence and vandalism are threatening passengers’ well-being, while the lack of investment in security and video surveillance systems makes people feel even more unsafe. These issues need to be addressed through targeted investments in infrastructure and public transport. In view of the above: 1.

What support will the Commission offer Member States to curb the growing number of attacks on frontline staff and facilitate psychophysical therapy and legal assistance programmes for workers affected by such incidents?
What will it do to encourage investment in infrastructure and public transport so video surveillance systems can be installed and safety at work improved?

Does it think it would be appropriate to make it mandatory for any new public transport vehicles being purchased to have minimum safety equipment, such as a ‘closed cab’ isolating the driver from the rest of the vehicle, so as to ensure uniform safety standards across the Union?
answer: 1. The Commission provides a framework to exchange information, knowledge and best practices at the Expert Group for Land Transport Security which fosters ongoing exchanges of relevant experience, policies and practices between the Member States and the various parties involved. 2.

The Expert Group on Urban Mobility set up by the Commission and composed of representatives from Member States, cities and regions and stakeholders organisations, includes a dedicated subgroup for public transport that is working on recommendations to all levels of governance on various topics. This includes e.g.

how to prioritise public transport (safety being an important aspect for both users and transport workers) and how to ensure the long-term sustainability of the sector in terms of funding and investments. The first set of recommendations has been recently publishe d (2) and more are intended to follow in the course of 2024. 3.

Motor vehicles, including buses for public transport of passengers, must be type-approved in order to be placed on the market, registered or entered into service on the territory of the Member States. However, the EU type approval rules (3) do not as such take into account the specific purpose for which a particular vehicle will be used after its registration.

Security risks can diverge greatly on the basis of the location and the type of transport services (e.g. urban, rural, intercity, occasional, etc.) The Commission considers that a priori it would be disproportionate to require at EU level all buses to be equipped with closed cabs on mandatory base without further assessing the specific circumstances and the concrete risks involved.
